claims.claim: Rituals, also called rites, are performative acts by which practitioners carry out religious beliefs; they follow a formal order or sequence (a liturgical order), are performed in a setting set apart as sacred during the time of performance, and are inherently social and learned rather than idiosyncratic.

Religious rituals are behaviors or practices that are required or expected of the members of a particular group; some form of religion is found in every known culture and is usually practiced publicly by a group, and funeral rites are practiced in every culture in some way, with common elements such as announcement of the death, care of the deceased, disposition, and ceremony.

Arnold van Gennep, a French anthropologist and folklorist, coined the phrase 'rites of passage' in 1909 and described three consecutive stages: separation, transition, and incorporation, also called preliminal, liminal, and postliminal stages (limen is Latin for 'threshold').

Victor Turner's later work (1969) analyzed liminality in detail, describing the liminal individual as 'betwixt and between' statuses and outside ordinary social structure, and noting that a cohort passing through a rite together shares a strong bond of equality that scholars call communitas.

Rites of passage mark changes in social status and are commonly associated with birth, maturity or coming of age, marriage, and death; they exist in all historically known societies and can be secular as well as religious, with examples such as graduation ceremonies and civil-religious marriages.

Rites of intensification, also called rites of affirmation or calendrical rites, are recurring rites performed to affirm, strengthen, and maintain bonds of solidarity through stable, repetitive structure; commemoration feasts are typically held over a calendrical cycle of about a year.

Pilgrimage is a journey undertaken for a religious motive toward a place that has been sanctified by association with a divinity or other holy personage; the institution is evident in all world religions, and pilgrimages commonly involve separation from the everyday world, fixed sacred times, and ritual movements at the site itself.

Scholars frame rituals as serving social functions: fostering solidarity and identity within a community of believers (associated with Durkheim), marking time through recurring calendrical observances, expressing and carrying out beliefs through symbolic action, and easing individuals through changes of status without social disruption (van Gennep's account of rites of passage).

Ritual is distinct from routine: unlike idiosyncratic behaviors an individual may practice on their own, rituals are learned and shared, follow a formal order, and are set apart as sacred during performance; even a ritual performed alone, such as walking a labyrinth, connects the performer to a larger community.

Scholars describe secular ritual: there are secular rites of passage such as graduation, and Robert Bellah (1967) documented civil religion, in which civic ceremonies such as presidential inaugurations, flag-raising and half-mast observances, and national funerary honors use sacred language and ritual forms to elevate the nation as a sacred entity.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Naming of the three stages of rites of passage varies across sources.
positions: OpenStax Introduction to Anthropology (following van Gennep) names separation, transition, and incorporation, with the transition stage called liminality.
Britannica's rite of passage article names separation, transition, and reincorporation, labeled preliminal, liminal, and postliminal stages.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All sources agree on a three-stage structure centered on a threshold (limen). The lesson presents separation, liminality (transition), and incorporation, and notes the preliminal/liminal/postliminal labels, since liminality is the standard scholarly term for the middle stage and the one used in Turner's analysis.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Scholars define ritual with different emphases.
positions: Durkheim's approach ties religious practices to 'sacred things' set apart and to the moral community they unite.
Geertz's symbolic approach emphasizes systems of symbols that shape moods and motivations.
Functionalist accounts emphasize what rituals do for groups, such as producing solidarity and cohesion.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents a working definition (formal, structured, repeatable acts carrying symbolic meaning for a community) as one scholarly framing and notes that definitions vary; it stays descriptive and does not adjudicate between schools.

sourceRecords.title: 15.1 The Sociological Approach to Religion — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Existing source-registry record reused (identical id and URL). Read live on 2026-08-21 for this lesson. Supports: religious rituals as behaviors or practices required or expected of group members; religion as found in every known culture and usually practiced publicly by a group; funeral rites as a cultural universal with common elements (announcement, care of the deceased, disposition, ceremony); feasts and festivals among religious practices; functionalist framing of religion's role in group cohesion and meaning. Reference only; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: 13.4 Rituals of Transition and Conformity — Introduction to Anthropology
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: rituals/rites as performative acts following a liturgical order, performed in a set-apart sacred setting, inherently social and learned rather than idiosyncratic; rites of passage identified by van Gennep in 1909 with stages separation (preliminal), transition/liminality, incorporation (postliminal); Turner's liminality as 'betwixt and between' and communitas; rites of intensification (also rites of affirmation, calendrical rites) with repetitive structure; commemoration feasts held over a yearly calendrical cycle; rites of affliction and rites of rebellion as additional categories; secular rites of passage (graduation, quinceanera, civil-religious marriage); the observation that rituals are never exactly duplicated. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: 13.5 Other Forms of Religious Practice — Introduction to Anthropology
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports the brief treatment of secular ritual: secular religion as a system of beliefs elevating social ideas or the nation to a semidivine status; Robert Bellah (1967) documenting American civil religion, with presidential inaugurations, convocation of Congress, flag rituals (raising, half-mast, draping coffins), and national cemeteries such as Arlington using sacred language and ritual forms to elevate the nation-state. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Rite of Passage
sourceRecords.provider: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Edward Norbeck; Bobby C. Alexander)
sourceRecords.notes: Live site bot-blocks automated fetch; read the Internet Archive capture of 2021-11-02 (web.archive.org/web/20211102094238/https://www.britannica.com/topic/rite-of-passage); a newer 2024-12-23 capture gates the full article behind a paywall. Supports: rite of passage as a ceremonial event existing in all historically known societies that marks passage from one social or religious status to another; connection with the life milestones of birth, maturity, reproduction, and death; van Gennep (French anthropologist and folklorist) presenting the first substantial interpretation and coining the phrase 'rites of passage' in 1909; three consecutive elements of separation, transition, and reincorporation, labeled preliminal, liminal, and postliminal stages (limen, Latin for 'threshold'); van Gennep's view that rites ease individuals through transitions without social disruption; passage rites as historically primary socially approved vehicles for art, music, song, dance, and entertainment. Facts synthesized; no source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Pilgrimage
sourceRecords.notes: Live site bot-blocks automated fetch; read the Internet Archive capture of 2022-01-15 (web.archive.org/web/20220115165845/https://www.britannica.com/topic/pilgrimage-religion). Supports: pilgrimage as a journey undertaken for a religious motive, with pilgrims commonly seeking a specific place sanctified by association with a divinity or other holy personage; the institution of pilgrimage as evident in all world religions and in the religions of ancient Greece and Rome; recurring structural features across traditions, including separation from the everyday world (special clothing or abstention), the linking of sacred place with sacred time (fixed pilgrimage dates, annual festivals), and ritual movements at the site (circumambulation, Stations of the Cross); and the sense that a place can provide privileged access to a divine or transcendent sphere. Facts synthesized; no source wording reproduced.
